title: Given a list of employee names, return a list of their lengths.
shortTitle: Given a list of employee names, return a list of their lengths

s1_definition.profdef: This is a `map` from `String` to `Integer`, applying `String.length()` to each name to produce a stream of lengths. For primitive efficiency you can use `mapToInt(String::length)`, which yields an `IntStream` and avoids boxing each length into an `Integer` object.
s1_definition.analogy: The forms officer at the National Bank of India is designing name boxes on a printed form and needs to know how many characters each name has so the boxes fit. She counts the letters in each name and writes the count. `map` with length is exactly that counting.
s1_definition.oneliner: `map(String::length)` turns each name into its character count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a `map` from `String` to `Integer`, applying `String.length()` to each name to produce a stream of lengths. For primitive efficiency you can use `mapToInt(String::length)`, which yields an `IntStream` and avoids boxing each length into an `Integer` object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The forms officer at the National Bank of India is designing name boxes on a printed form and needs to know how many characters each name has so the boxes fit. She counts the letters in each name and writes the count. `map` with length is exactly that counting.

**One line to remember:** `map(String::length)` turns each name into its character count.

sections.s2_technical:
The `String.length()` method returns the number of characters in the string as an int. Applying it through map, as `map(String::length)`, transforms a stream of names into a stream of lengths, one length per name, so it is a one-to-one transformation and the result has the same number of elements as the input.

There is a subtlety about boxing. The regular `map` produces a `Stream<Integer>`, which means each primitive int length is wrapped in an Integer object, costing memory and a little time. Java provides `mapToInt(String::length)`, which produces an `IntStream` of raw ints with no boxing. On large datasets the IntStream is more efficient and also unlocks convenient numeric terminals like `sum`, `average`, and `max` directly.

If you need the final result as a `List<Integer>` you can box back at the end with `boxed().collect(Collectors.toList())`, or if you only need statistics you stay in the primitive IntStream and call something like `summaryStatistics()`. The choice depends on whether the caller wants a list of lengths or an aggregate.

A senior nuance: for text with characters outside the basic range — emoji or certain scripts — `length()` counts UTF-16 code units, not visual characters, so a single emoji can report length two. For employee names this rarely matters, but a senior engineer knows the distinction between code units and code points when correctness over arbitrary Unicode is required.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is printing personalised cheque books and the design team needs the character length of each account holder's name to size the printed name field correctly, since a very long name needs a smaller font. We have the list of names and must produce the matching list of lengths. This is exactly how a map to length works — each name is transformed into its character count, producing a parallel list of lengths.

The code works with a list of name strings directly. A `NameMetricsService` exposes `nameLengths(List<String>)` using mapToInt then boxing to a list. The runnable `Main` feeds names of varying length and logs the lengths.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four names — Rajesh, Priya, Amit, Indira.

Step 1: The stream opens over four name strings.

Step 2: mapToInt applies length to Rajesh, which has six characters, producing the raw int 6 in an IntStream with no boxing.

Step 3: Priya has five characters, producing 5.

Step 4: Amit has four characters, producing 4.

Step 5: Indira has six characters, producing 6.

Step 6: boxed converts the IntStream of raw ints into a Stream of Integer objects, and collect gathers them into a list of lengths in the same order as the names.

```
Oct 30, 2026 11:50:04 AM com.bank.metrics.service.NameMetricsService nameLengths
INFO: Computing lengths for 4 names
Oct 30, 2026 11:50:04 AM com.bank.metrics.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Name lengths: [6, 5, 4, 6]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Stream<String> ["Rajesh","Priya","Amit","Indira"]
    │
    ▼
  mapToInt(String::length)  → IntStream [6, 5, 4, 6]   (raw ints, no boxing)
    ├─ "Rajesh" → 6
    ├─ "Priya"  → 5
    ├─ "Amit"   → 4
    └─ "Indira" → 6
    │
    ▼
  .boxed()  → Stream<Integer> [6,5,4,6]
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  List<Integer> [6,5,4,6]  (parallel to input order)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — map to length ═══

  ┌─ Primitive efficiency ───────────────────────────────┐
  │ map(String::length)   → Stream<Integer> (boxes)      │
  │ mapToInt(String::length) → IntStream (no box)        │
  │ IntStream unlocks sum()/average()/max() directly     │
  │ length() counts UTF-16 code units, not glyphs        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          NameMetricsService          │
  │ ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │ + nameLengths(List<String>)          │
  │     : List<Integer>                  │
  │   mapToInt → boxed → toList          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for nameLengths:
    Pre:  list non-null, names non-null
    Post: lengths list parallels input order, same size
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To turn each name into its character count I map with the string length method, which transforms a stream of names into a stream of lengths, one length per name, so the result is the same size as the input. For this I preferred mapToInt rather than the ordinary map, because mapToInt produces a primitive IntStream with no boxing, whereas ordinary map would wrap every length in an Integer object, costing memory and a little time on large datasets.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was for printing personalised cheque books. The design team needed each account holder's name length to size the printed name field, because a very long name needs a smaller font, so I streamed the names and mapped each to its length, then boxed back to a list of integers at the very end.

A senior point I always mention is the benefit of staying in the primitive IntStream: beyond avoiding boxing, it unlocks numeric terminals like sum, average, and max directly, so if the design team later wanted the longest name or the average length I could compute it without converting back. I also note a correctness subtlety — the length method counts UTF-16 code units, not visual characters, so a single emoji or certain scripts can report a length of two. For ordinary employee names this never matters, but knowing the difference between code units and code points is what lets me reason correctly when a field must handle arbitrary Unicode.
